boundaries.evidence:
def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel: d=1 and L=0 are admitted. L=0 forces a constant two-variable kernel, not necessarily the zero kernel; K=0 is allowed and satisfies the growth estimate. The kernel inequality includes coincident arguments and zero vectors. It quantifies every pair directly and has no time endpoint or selection construction. This disposition separates an empty/zero admissible object from an empty input domain; it does not exclude the former by a generic nonemptiness claim. Exact current Definition anchor: Let $d\ge1$, with the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. An interaction kernel is a continuous map $K:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. It is globally Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the convention used on this page if
$$|K(x,y)-K(x',y')|\le L(|x-x'|+|y-y'|)$$
for all $x,y,x',y'\in\mathbb R^d$. This implies the linear-growth estimate
$$|K(x,y)|\le |K(0,0)|+L(|x|+|y|).$$
The notation $L$ always refers to this two-variable convention; the stability factor below is therefore $2L$.

boundaries.evidence:
def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel: The mollifier has unit mass, so an empty support/zero mollifier is excluded. The scaled family is for positive epsilon; epsilon=0 is not substituted into epsilon^-2 rho(z/epsilon). Exact current Definition anchor: In two dimensions let $z^\perp=(-z_2,z_1)$ and
$$G(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\log|z|,\qquad K(z)=\nabla^\perp G(z)=\frac{z^\perp}{2\pi|z|^2}\quad(z\ne0).$$
The locally integrable value assigned to $K(0)$ is immaterial. Fix a radial, nonnegative smooth bump $\rho$ supported in the unit ball with $\int\rho=1$; its scaled family is the mollifier family of [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]]. Put $\rho_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-2}\rho(z/\varepsilon)$, $G_\varepsilon=G*\rho_\varepsilon$, and
$$K_\varepsilon=K*\rho_\varepsilon.$$
The kernel is a regularized interaction; its smoothness and global Lipschitz property are proved in a separate lemma. It does not define the singular physical interaction at a collision.

citations.quote:
1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect
to this metric*, always.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

derivations.claim:
Let $(X_n)$ be Cauchy in $d_{\mathcal X}$. By [A1], choose measurable representatives and, for each representative, a measurable conull set on which its paths are continuous. Countable Choice gives these sets simultaneously; their intersection $C\in\mathcal A$ is conull. For a fixed countable dense set $D\subseteq[0,T]$, continuity on $C$ gives
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_m(t,z)-X_n(t,z)|=\sup_{q\in D}|X_m(q,z)-X_n(q,z)|\qquad(z\in C).$$
Each fixed-time section of each coordinate is measurable by [F6], since coordinate projections are continuous, and the right side is measurable by [F5]. Define it to be zero on $C^c$; this is a measurable representative of the time-supremum difference, as prescribed in the Statement. Changing the conull set or the representative does not change its integral. Symmetry and the triangle inequality follow pointwise on a common conull set, and a zero distance forces the paths to agree almost everywhere: for a nonnegative measurable supremum $g$ with zero integral, $\mu\{g>1/j\}\le j\int g=0$ for every $j\ge1$. It is integrable because on $C$ it is bounded by the sum of the two given integrable path suprema.

Choose increasing indices $n_k$ successively as the least indices large enough that $\|X_m-X_n\|_{\mathcal X}\le2^{-k}$ whenever $m,n\ge n_k$. Put $g_k(z)=\sup_t|X_{n_{k+1}}(t,z)-X_{n_k}(t,z)|$ on $C$ and $g_k(z)=0$ off $C$. By step 1.1 each $g_k$ is measurable and $\int_Eg_k\,d\mu\le2^{-k}$. Thus $G=\sum_{k=1}^\infty g_k$ is measurable by [F5], and Tonelli gives $\int_EG\,d\mu\le\sum_{k=1}^\infty2^{-k}<\infty$. By [F7], $A:=C\cap\{G<\infty\}$ is measurable and conull. For every $z\in A$, the paths $X_{n_k}(\cdot,z)$ are uniformly Cauchy on $[0,T]$.

Replace each selected representative by $\widetilde X_{n_k}(t,z)=X_{n_k}(t,z)$ on $A$ and $0$ outside $A$. These maps remain jointly measurable and represent the same equivalence classes. By [F1], for each $z\in A$ their uniform limit is a continuous path $X(\cdot,z)$; set $X(\cdot,z)=0$ off $A$. The coordinate projections of $\widetilde X_{n_k}$ are measurable, so their pointwise limits are measurable by [F5]; [F6] makes the resulting map into $\mathbb R^d$ jointly measurable. Its time-supremum function is measurable because its paths are continuous and the supremum equals the countable supremum over $D$ of measurable sections. On $A$, $\sup_t|X_t-\widetilde X_{n_k,t}|\le\sum_{j\ge k}g_j$; off $A$ this difference is zero. Hence the integrable series tail bounds $\|X-X_{n_k}\|_{\mathcal X}$ and tends to zero. Since $X_{n_k}$ has finite norm, [F4] gives $\|X\|_{\mathcal X}<\infty$.

Since the original sequence is Cauchy and its subsequence converges to $X$, the triangle inequality gives $\|X_n-X\|_{\mathcal X}\to0$: for any $\epsilon>0$, first take $k$ with $\|X_{n_k}-X\|<\epsilon/2$, then take $n$ beyond the Cauchy index so $\|X_n-X_{n_k}\|<\epsilon/2$. Thus every Cauchy sequence converges, which is completeness by [F3].

Query the oracle at every grid point in lexicographic order with $i$ first and $j$ second, storing the returned values. def-characteristic-mean-field-solution: The initial law is a probability measure, so it is nonempty, not the zero signed measure. A single Dirac initial law is allowed. The kernel can be0, giving constant paths satisfying the equation. The equation includes t=0, where its time integral is0 and X0(x)=x; t=T is included. The definition specifies a given map up to a null set, not a choice of an optimizer. This disposition separates an empty/zero admissible object from an empty input domain; it does not exclude the former by a generic nonemptiness claim. Exact current Definition anchor: Fix $T>0$, a globally Lipschitz kernel $K$ as in [[def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel]], and a Borel probability measure $\mu_0$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moment as in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]]. A characteristic solution on $[0,T]$ consists of a jointly Borel map $X:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, defined up to a $\mu_0$-null set of labels, such that $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ is absolutely continuous for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$, $X_0(x)=x$, and
$$X_t(x)=x+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(X_s(x),X_s(y))\,d\mu_0(y)\,ds$$
for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$. It transports $\mu_0$ to $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$, where $(X_t)_\#\mu_0(A):=\mu_0(X_t^{-1}(A))$. The weighted path integrability convention is $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(x)|d\mu_0(x)<\infty$; in particular every time slice has finite first moment.

def-mean-field-and-weighted-vortex-particle-systems: N>=1 excludes an empty empirical probability sum and includes N=1. Real signed weights may be0; all zero weights give zero signed vorticity and zero weighted velocity. Exact current Definition anchor: For a globally Lipschitz interaction kernel $K$ and $N\ge1$, the equal-probability mean-field particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K(x_i(t),x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.$$
Its empirical probability measure is $\mu_N(t)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$.

For a mollified two-dimensional Biot-Savart kernel $K_\varepsilon$ from [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]] and real weights $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_N$, the weighted signed vortex particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\sum_{j=1}^N\Gamma_jK_\varepsilon(x_i(t)-x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,$$
with vorticity measure $\omega_N(t)=\sum_i\Gamma_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$. If $\Gamma_i=1/N$ and $K(x,y)=K_\varepsilon(x-y)$, the first system is the probability special case. The weighted signed system is a first-order Biot-Savart model.
Definition addresses the one boundary in the stated domain: N\ge1.

def-signed-vorticity-characteristic-solution: AC is explicitly assumed. The Definition treats M=0 first by a constant zero measure curve, avoiding division by M. Only when M>0 is the signed-label probability lambda0 formed. Exact current Definition anchor: Assume AC. Let $\omega_0$ be a finite signed Borel measure on $\mathbb R^2$, set $M=|\omega_0|(\mathbb R^2)$, and let $\omega_0=\omega_0^+-\omega_0^-$ be its Jordan decomposition. The Jordan total-variation formula gives $M=\omega_0^+(\mathbb R^2)+\omega_0^-(\mathbb R^2)$. If $M=0$, its characteristic solution is the constant zero measure curve. If $M>0$, set $E=\mathbb R^2\times\{+1,-1\}$ with sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)\otimes 2^{\{+1,-1\}}$, and define the probability measure $\lambda_0$ by $\lambda_0(A\times\{s\})=\omega_0^s(A)/M$ for Borel $A$ and $s\in\{+1,-1\}$; its total mass is one by the displayed formula. A signed characteristic solution for the regularized kernel $K_\varepsilon$ on $[0,T]$ is a jointly measurable path map $Z:[0,T]\times E\to\mathbb R^2$, modulo $\lambda_0$-almost everywhere equality, with absolutely continuous paths for almost every label, $Z_0(x,s)=x$, and

$$Z_t(x,s)=x+M\int_0^t\int_E rK_\varepsilon(Z_u(x,s)-Z_u(y,r))\,d\lambda_0(y,r)\,du,$$

such that its time-supremum function is measurable and $\int_E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|Z_t(x,s)|\,d\lambda_0(x,s)<\infty$. It represents the signed measure curve

$$\omega_t=M\int_E s\,\delta_{Z_t(x,s)}\,d\lambda_0(x,s).$$

Here $\omega_0^s$ denotes $\omega_0^+$ when $s=+1$ and $\omega_0^-$ when $s=-1$. The total variation mass is $M$ at time zero, and the sign coordinate records each Jordan part separately.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], $G_\varepsilon$ and $K_\varepsilon$ are smooth and $DK_\varepsilon(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}K(x-z)D\rho_\varepsilon(z)dz,$ componentwise. The gradient $D\rho_\varepsilon$ is supported in $|z|\le\varepsilon$ and satisfies $\|D\rho_\varepsilon\|_\infty=\varepsilon^{-3}\|D\rho\|_\infty$. If $|x|\le2\varepsilon$, then $|x-z|\le3\varepsilon$. Since $|K(w)|\le(2\pi|w|)^{-1}$, polar integration [F2] gives $\int_{|w|\le3\varepsilon}|K(w)|dw\le C\varepsilon$. Thus $\|DK_\varepsilon(x)\|\le C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}$ in this region.

If $|x|>2\varepsilon$ and $|z|\le\varepsilon$, then $|x-z|>|x|/2$ and $|K(x-z)|\le C/|x|$. Scaling [F3] gives $\|D\rho_\varepsilon\|_1=\varepsilon^{-1}\|D\rho\|_1$, so $\|DK_\varepsilon(x)\|\le \frac{C}{|x|}\|D\rho_\varepsilon\|_1\le C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}.$ Combining this with step 1.1 yields the global derivative bound.

Apply [F4] to the smooth map $K_\varepsilon$ along the segment between any $x,y\in\mathbb R^2$. The derivative bound in step 2.1 gives $|K_\varepsilon(x)-K_\varepsilon(y)|\le C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}|x-y|.$ This is the claimed global Lipschitz property.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then there exist positive
measures $
u^+,
u^-:(X,\mathcal A)	o[0,+\infty]$, at least one finite on $X$, such that
$$
u=
u^+-
u^-,$$
and $
u^+\perp 
u^-$.

These measures are unique: if $
u=\mu-\eta$ with positive measures
$\mu\perp\eta$, then $\mu=
u^+$ and $\eta=
u^-$.

The following conditional assertion is choice-free: if a Hahn partition
$X=P\sqcup N$ is supplied, the formulas $
u^+(E)=
u(E\cap P)$ and
$
u^-(E)=-
u(E\cap N)$ construct these unique measures. Comparing
two supplied mutually singular positive decompositions also requires no AC.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on

Let $d\ge1$, with the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. An interaction kernel is a continuous map $K:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. It is globally Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the convention used on this page if
$$|K(x,y)-K(x',y')|\le L(|x-x'|+|y-y'|)$$
for all $x,y,x',y'\in\mathbb R^d$. This implies the linear-growth estimate
$$|K(x,y)|\le |K(0,0)|+L(|x|+|y|).$$
The notation $L$ always refers to this two-variable convention; the stability factor below is therefore $2L$.

Fix $T>0$, a globally Lipschitz kernel $K$ as in [[def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel]], and a Borel probability measure $\mu_0$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moment as in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]]. A characteristic solution on $[0,T]$ consists of a jointly Borel map $X:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, defined up to a $\mu_0$-null set of labels, such that $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ is absolutely continuous for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$, $X_0(x)=x$, and
$$X_t(x)=x+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(X_s(x),X_s(y))\,d\mu_0(y)\,ds$$
for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$. It transports $\mu_0$ to $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$, where $(X_t)_\#\mu_0(A):=\mu_0(X_t^{-1}(A))$. The weighted path integrability convention is $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(x)|d\mu_0(x)<\infty$; in particular every time slice has finite first moment.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

If $\mu,
u$ are Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moments, then $\Pi(\mu,
u)$ is nonempty and $W_1(\mu,
u)<\infty$ for the definition in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

derivations.claim: Fix any $\pi_0\in\Pi(\mu_0,\nu_0)$ and transport it by the two flows: $\pi_t=(X_t,Y_t)_\#\pi_0.$ Its marginals are $\mu_t,\nu_t$. Set $D(t)=\int|X_t(x)-Y_t(y)|d\pi_0(x,y)$. This is finite and continuous by the first moments, the integrable path suprema, and [F5].

For each initial pair, subtract the characteristic equations and apply [F1]. Integrating over $\pi_0$ yields $D(t)\le D(0)+2L\int_0^tD(s)ds,$ because the first coordinate difference contributes $LD(s)$, while the averaged interaction-coordinate difference contributes another $LD(s)$ by the marginal identities of $\pi_0$. Applying [L1] gives $D(t)\le e^{2Lt}D(0)$. Since $\pi_t$ is an admissible coupling, [F3] implies $W_1(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{2Lt}\int|x-y|d\pi_0$.
The inequality in step 2.1 holds for every $\pi_0\in\Pi(\mu_0,\nu_0)$. Taking the infimum of its right side gives the Statement by the definition of $W_1$ in [F3]; no minimizer is required.

For a globally Lipschitz interaction kernel $K$ and $N\ge1$, the equal-probability mean-field particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K(x_i(t),x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.$$
Its empirical probability measure is $\mu_N(t)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$.

For a mollified two-dimensional Biot-Savart kernel $K_\varepsilon$ from [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]] and real weights $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_N$, the weighted signed vortex particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\sum_{j=1}^N\Gamma_jK_\varepsilon(x_i(t)-x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,$$
with vorticity measure $\omega_N(t)=\sum_i\Gamma_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$. If $\Gamma_i=1/N$ and $K(x,y)=K_\varepsilon(x-y)$, the first system is the probability special case. The weighted signed system is a first-order Biot-Savart model.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By [F2] and [F1], $\frac{d}{dt}\frac1N\sum_i\varphi(x_i(t))=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}\nabla\varphi(x_i(t))\cdot K(x_i(t),x_j(t)).$ The double sum is finite, so integration in time gives the left side of the Statement as its time integral.

Expanding both empirical integrals on the right of the Statement gives exactly the same finite double sum as in step 1.1. This proves the identity for every $t$ and includes repeated particle positions without a distinctness assumption.

Let $d\ge1$, with the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. An interaction kernel is a continuous map $K:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. It is globally Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the convention used on this page if
$$|K(x,y)-K(x',y')|\le L(|x-x'|+|y-y'|)$$
for all $x,y,x',y'\in\mathbb R^d$. This implies the linear-growth estimate
$$|K(x,y)|\le |K(0,0)|+L(|x|+|y|).$$
The notation $L$ always refers to this two-variable convention; the stability factor below is therefore $2L$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(E,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a probability space, $T>0$, and $d\ge1$. Use the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Let $\mathcal X$ be the space, modulo equality $\mu$-almost everywhere, of jointly measurable maps $X:[0,T]\times E\to\mathbb R^d$ whose paths are continuous for almost every label and whose time-supremum function is measurable, and for which
$$\|X\|_{\mathcal X}:=\int_E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(z)|d\mu(z)<\infty.$$
In this formula and in $\|X-Y\|_{\mathcal X}$, take the supremum on a measurable conull set where the relevant paths are continuous and extend it by zero off that set; equality almost everywhere means equality of whole paths outside one measurable null set. The seminorm identifies maps equal almost everywhere, and the induced distance $d_{\mathcal X}(X,Y)=\|X-Y\|_{\mathcal X}$ is a metric on the quotient; it is complete.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

derivations.claim: On a time interval $[a,a+\delta]$, use the space in [F2] over $(\mathbb R^d,\mu_0)$ and fix the initial label map $X_a$. Define $\Phi(Z)_t(x)=X_a(x)+\int_a^t\int K(Z_s(x),Z_s(y))d\mu_0(y)ds.$ The growth bound in [F1], the integrability of $X_a$, and [F4] make the time integral finite in the weighted norm. For almost every label, the integrand is continuous in time; it is dominated in the second label by $|K(0,0)|+L(\sup_s|Z_s(x)|+\sup_s|Z_s(y)|)$, integrable by the path norm, so [F5] makes each output path continuous. The space is nonempty because the constant-in-time path $X_a$ belongs to it.

For any $Z,W$, applying [F1], integrating first over the label $x$ and then $y$, and using that $\mu_0$ has mass one gives $\|\Phi Z-\Phi W\|\le2L\delta\|Z-W\|.$ Choose $\delta>0$ with $2L\delta<1$ when $L>0$; if $L=0$ any finite $\delta$ works. The contraction theorem [F3] yields a unique fixed point on this interval.

The bound in step 2.1 applies on each successive interval with the attained endpoint path as initial data. By [F6], choose an integer $J>2LT$ and partition $[0,T]$ into $J$ equal intervals (or use one interval when $L=0$); each interval then has length below $1/(2L)$ and successive fixed points construct the solution on all of $[0,T]$. Each fixed point belongs to the weighted path space, so its endpoint has finite first moment and is admissible for the next interval.

Any two solutions on the first interval are fixed points of the same contraction and hence agree by [F3]. Repeating on each successive interval gives equality for $\mu_0$-almost every label on all of $[0,T]$. The fixed point equation and the pushforward definition give exactly the characteristic solution in [F1] and [[def-characteristic-mean-field-solution]].

Fix $T>0$, a globally Lipschitz kernel $K$ as in [[def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel]], and a Borel probability measure $\mu_0$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moment as in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]]. A characteristic solution on $[0,T]$ consists of a jointly Borel map $X:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, defined up to a $\mu_0$-null set of labels, such that $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ is absolutely continuous for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$, $X_0(x)=x$, and
$$X_t(x)=x+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(X_s(x),X_s(y))\,d\mu_0(y)\,ds$$
for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$. It transports $\mu_0$ to $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$, where $(X_t)_\#\mu_0(A):=\mu_0(X_t^{-1}(A))$. The weighted path integrability convention is $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(x)|d\mu_0(x)<\infty$; in particular every time slice has finite first moment.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: For $\mu_0$-almost every label $x$, the path $X_s(x)$ is absolutely continuous. For a fixed label, its velocity is continuous in time: the integrand converges pointwise for almost every second label and is dominated by the integrable path supremum in the definition, so [F5] applies. Thus its path is $C^1$, and the ordinary chain rule [F2] and defining ODE [F1] give $\varphi(X_t(x))-\varphi(x)=\int_0^t\nabla\varphi(X_s(x))\cdot\int K(X_s(x),X_s(y))d\mu_0(y)ds.$ The integrand is absolutely integrable over time and both labels: $\nabla\varphi$ is bounded, and [F1] bounds $|K(X_s(x),X_s(y))|$ by a constant plus $L(|X_s(x)|+|X_s(y)|)$, whose label integrals are finite uniformly in $s$. This last bound and [F4] justify the exchanges; [F5] supplies the stated velocity continuity.

Integrate step 1.1 in $x$ against $\mu_0$. The left side becomes the two displayed measure integrals by the pushforward formula [F1]. By [F3] and the absolute-integrability check in step 1.1, exchange the time and label integrals. Replacing $X_s(x),X_s(y)$ by their pushforward variables gives the right side of the Statement.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In two dimensions let $z^\perp=(-z_2,z_1)$ and
$$G(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\log|z|,\qquad K(z)=\nabla^\perp G(z)=\frac{z^\perp}{2\pi|z|^2}\quad(z\ne0).$$
The locally integrable value assigned to $K(0)$ is immaterial. Fix a radial, nonnegative smooth bump $\rho$ supported in the unit ball with $\int\rho=1$; its scaled family is the mollifier family of [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]]. Put $\rho_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-2}\rho(z/\varepsilon)$, $G_\varepsilon=G*\rho_\varepsilon$, and
$$K_\varepsilon=K*\rho_\varepsilon.$$
The kernel is a regularized interaction; its smoothness and global Lipschitz property are proved in a separate lemma. It does not define the singular physical interaction at a collision.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: On $|x|\le2\varepsilon$, [F2] and $|K(x)|\le(2\pi|x|)^{-1}$ give $\int_{|x|\le2\varepsilon}|K(x)|dx\le C\varepsilon$. Also $|K_\varepsilon(x)|\le\|\rho_\varepsilon\|_\infty\int_{|w|\le3\varepsilon}|K(w)|dw\le C_\rho/\varepsilon,$ so its integral over this disk is at most $C_\rho\varepsilon$.

First, each component $z_j\rho_\varepsilon(z)$ is integrable because it is bounded and compactly supported. Radiality makes it odd under the reflection $z\mapsto-z$; applying [F4] to that reflection, whose Jacobian determinant has absolute value one, gives $\int z_j\rho_\varepsilon(z)\,dz=-\int z_j\rho_\varepsilon(z)\,dz$, hence every first-moment component is zero. Now fix $|x|>2\varepsilon$ and $|z|\le\varepsilon$. The segment from $x$ to $x-z$ is contained in the open ball $B_{|x|/2}(x)$, which is convex and avoids the origin, and each second coordinate derivative of $K(w)=w^\perp/(2\pi|w|^2)$ is bounded there by $C|x|^{-3}$: direct differentiation gives terms of the forms $c\,w_i|w|^{-4}$ and $c\,w_iw_jw_k|w|^{-6}$. Apply the scalar Taylor theorem [F3] to each component of $K$ along this segment. The coordinate remainders are each bounded by $C|z|^2|x|^{-3}$, so [F5] gives the vector bound $K(x-z)=K(x)-DK(x)z+R(x,z)$ with $|R(x,z)|\le C|z|^2|x|^{-3}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then there exist positive
measures $
u^+,
u^-:(X,\mathcal A)	o[0,+\infty]$, at least one finite on $X$, such that
$$
u=
u^+-
u^-,$$
and $
u^+\perp 
u^-$.

These measures are unique: if $
u=\mu-\eta$ with positive measures
$\mu\perp\eta$, then $\mu=
u^+$ and $\eta=
u^-$.

The following conditional assertion is choice-free: if a Hahn partition
$X=P\sqcup N$ is supplied, the formulas $
u^+(E)=
u(E\cap P)$ and
$
u^-(E)=-
u(E\cap N)$ construct these unique measures. Comparing
two supplied mutually singular positive decompositions also requires no AC.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and the mollifier of [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]]. For every $\varepsilon>0$, $G_\varepsilon$ and $K_\varepsilon$ are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and there is $C_\rho<\infty$ independent of $\varepsilon$ such that
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}\|DK_\varepsilon(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}.$$
Consequently $K_\varepsilon$ is globally Lipschitz with constant at most $C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}$.

Assume AC for the Jordan decompositions in [[def-signed-split-transport-cost]]. If finite signed measures $\omega,
u$ have the same positive-part mass and the same negative-part mass, and their total variations have finite first moments, then the couplings in $C_{\pm}(\omega,
u)$ exist, $C_{\pm}(\omega,
u)<\infty$, and
$$d_{BL}(\omega,
u)\le C_{\pm}(\omega,
u).$$

$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}\|DK_\varepsilon(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}.$$
Consequently $K_\varepsilon$ is globally Lipschitz with constant at most $C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $\omega,
u$ be finite signed Borel measures on $\mathbb R^d$ such that $|\omega-
u|(\mathbb R^d)<\infty$. For each bounded Lipschitz test function, integration against $\omega-
u$ is defined by [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]; boundedness and finite total variation make every test in the following set integrable. Set $\|\phi\|_\infty:=\sup_x|\phi(x)|$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(\phi):=\sup_{x
e y}|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|/|x-y|$, using the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Define the bounded-Lipschitz dual discrepancy
$$d_{BL}(\omega,
u):=\sup\left\{\left|\int\phi\,d(\omega-
u)ight|:\|\phi\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}(\phi)\le1ight\}.$$
The integral bound by total variation shows this supremum is finite. This page uses only the displayed dual quantity and makes no separate metric-separation claim. No Jordan decomposition, positivity, or probability normalization is needed.

Assume $d\ge1$ and the Axiom of Choice when invoking [[thm-jordan-decomposition-for-signed-measures]]. Let $\omega,
u$ be finite signed Borel measures on $\mathbb R^d$ whose total variations have finite first moments, and use the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Write their Jordan parts as $\omega^+,\omega^-$ and $
u^+,
u^-$. If the positive-part masses agree and the negative-part masses agree, define using finite nonnegative Borel measures $\pi^\pm$ on $\mathbb R^d	imes\mathbb R^d$ whose first and second marginals are respectively the corresponding positive or negative Jordan parts:
$$C_{\pm}(\omega,
u):=\inf_{\pi^+,\pi^-}\left(\int|x-y|d\pi^+(x,y)+\int|x-y|d\pi^-(x,y)ight),$$
where $\pi^+$ ranges over finite nonnegative couplings of $\omega^+$ and $
u^+$, and $\pi^-$ over finite nonnegative couplings of $\omega^-$ and $
u^-$. The infimum is over both sign couplings independently. This cost is not the probability $W_1$.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

u_t=0$, so all conclusions hold. Suppose $M>0$. Fix the prescribed couplings $\pi_0^+,\pi_0^-$. Transport each by the corresponding two characteristic flows to obtain couplings $\pi_t^+,\pi_t^-$. Let $D(t)=\sum_{s\in\{+,-\}}\int|X_t^\omega(x,s)-X_t^

u_t)\le D(t)$. Integrable path suprema and [F6] make $D$ continuous.

u|+L_\varepsilon D(t)$: the first term uses total variation mass $M$, and the inner second-coordinate differences integrate to the two transported coupling costs whose sum is $D(t)$. The defects add at most $\eta_\omega+\eta_

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then there exist positive
measures $
u^+,
u^-:(X,\mathcal A)	o[0,+\infty]$, at least one finite on $X$, such that
$$
u=
u^+-
u^-,$$
and $
u^+\perp 
u^-$.

These measures are unique: if $
u=\mu-\eta$ with positive measures
$\mu\perp\eta$, then $\mu=
u^+$ and $\eta=
u^-$.

The following conditional assertion is choice-free: if a Hahn partition
$X=P\sqcup N$ is supplied, the formulas $
u^+(E)=
u(E\cap P)$ and
$
u^-(E)=-
u(E\cap N)$ construct these unique measures. Comparing
two supplied mutually singular positive decompositions also requires no AC.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(E,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a probability space, $T>0$, and $d\ge1$. Use the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Let $\mathcal X$ be the space, modulo equality $\mu$-almost everywhere, of jointly measurable maps $X:[0,T]\times E\to\mathbb R^d$ whose paths are continuous for almost every label and whose time-supremum function is measurable, and for which
$$\|X\|_{\mathcal X}:=\int_E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(z)|d\mu(z)<\infty.$$
In this formula and in $\|X-Y\|_{\mathcal X}$, take the supremum on a measurable conull set where the relevant paths are continuous and extend it by zero off that set; equality almost everywhere means equality of whole paths outside one measurable null set. The seminorm identifies maps equal almost everywhere, and the induced distance $d_{\mathcal X}(X,Y)=\|X-Y\|_{\mathcal X}$ is a metric on the quotient; it is complete.

Assume Countable Choice and the mollifier of [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]]. For every $\varepsilon>0$, $G_\varepsilon$ and $K_\varepsilon$ are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and there is $C_\rho<\infty$ independent of $\varepsilon$ such that
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}\|DK_\varepsilon(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}.$$
Consequently $K_\varepsilon$ is globally Lipschitz with constant at most $C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}$.

Assume AC. Let $\omega_0$ be a finite signed Borel measure on $\mathbb R^2$, set $M=|\omega_0|(\mathbb R^2)$, and let $\omega_0=\omega_0^+-\omega_0^-$ be its Jordan decomposition. The Jordan total-variation formula gives $M=\omega_0^+(\mathbb R^2)+\omega_0^-(\mathbb R^2)$. If $M=0$, its characteristic solution is the constant zero measure curve. If $M>0$, set $E=\mathbb R^2\times\{+1,-1\}$ with sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)\otimes 2^{\{+1,-1\}}$, and define the probability measure $\lambda_0$ by $\lambda_0(A\times\{s\})=\omega_0^s(A)/M$ for Borel $A$ and $s\in\{+1,-1\}$; its total mass is one by the displayed formula. A signed characteristic solution for the regularized kernel $K_\varepsilon$ on $[0,T]$ is a jointly measurable path map $Z:[0,T]\times E\to\mathbb R^2$, modulo $\lambda_0$-almost everywhere equality, with absolutely continuous paths for almost every label, $Z_0(x,s)=x$, and

$$Z_t(x,s)=x+M\int_0^t\int_E rK_\varepsilon(Z_u(x,s)-Z_u(y,r))\,d\lambda_0(y,r)\,du,$$

such that its time-supremum function is measurable and $\int_E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|Z_t(x,s)|\,d\lambda_0(x,s)<\infty$. It represents the signed measure curve

$$\omega_t=M\int_E s\,\delta_{Z_t(x,s)}\,d\lambda_0(x,s).$$

Here $\omega_0^s$ denotes $\omega_0^+$ when $s=+1$ and $\omega_0^-$ when $s=-1$. The total variation mass is $M$ at time zero, and the sign coordinate records each Jordan part separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(E,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a probability space, $T>0$, and $d\ge1$. Use the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Let $\mathcal X$ be the space, modulo equality $\mu$-almost everywhere, of jointly measurable maps $X:[0,T]\times E\to\mathbb R^d$ whose paths are continuous for almost every label and whose time-supremum function is measurable, and for which
$$\|X\|_{\mathcal X}:=\int_E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(z)|d\mu(z)<\infty.$$
In this formula and in $\|X-Y\|_{\mathcal X}$, take the supremum on a measurable conull set where the relevant paths are continuous and extend it by zero off that set; equality almost everywhere means equality of whole paths outside one measurable null set. The seminorm identifies maps equal almost everywhere, and the induced distance $d_{\mathcal X}(X,Y)=\|X-Y\|_{\mathcal X}$ is a metric on the quotient; it is complete.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$, with Jordan decomposition
$
u=
u^+-
u^-$. Then for every measurable $E$:

1. $$|
u|(E)=
u^+(E)+
u^-(E);$$
2. the same value is the supremum over finite measurable partitions of $E$;
3. $$
u^+(E)=\sup\{
u(F):F\subseteq E,\ F\in\mathcal A\};$$
4. $$
u^-(E)=-\inf\{
u(F):F\subseteq E,\ F\in\mathcal A\}.$$

Let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$, with Jordan decomposition
$
u=
u^+-
u^-$. Then for every measurable $E$:

1. $$|
u|(E)=
u^+(E)+
u^-(E);$$
2. the same value is the supremum over finite measurable partitions of $E$;
3. $$
u^+(E)=\sup\{
u(F):F\subseteq E,\ F\in\mathcal A\};$$
4. $$
u^-(E)=-\inf\{
u(F):F\subseteq E,\ F\in\mathcal A\}.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

derivations.claim: Let $M=|\omega_0|(\mathbb R^2)$. If $M=0$, [F7] implies $\omega_0=0$, the represented curve is zero by [F2], and $u_t=0$ has the identity flow; all claims follow. Hence suppose $M>0$. By [A1], write $\omega_0=\omega_0^+-\omega_0^-$ with mutually singular positive parts. The definition [F2] supplies the label probability $\lambda_0$ on $E=\mathbb R^2\times\{+1,-1\}$, with $\lambda_0(A\times\{s\})=\omega_0^s(A)/M$; [F8] and the assumed total-variation moment give its finite first moment.

On a subinterval $[a,a+T']$, use the weighted path space over $(E,\lambda_0)$ and fix the attained initial label map $Z_a$ (with $Z_0(x,s)=x$ at the first interval). The constant-in-time path $Z_a$ shows the space is nonempty. Define $\Phi(Z)_t(x,s)=Z_a(x,s)+M\int_a^t\int_E rK_\varepsilon(Z_u(x,s)-Z_u(y,r))d\lambda_0(y,r)du.$ Linear growth and the integrable path supremum make this a well-defined continuous-path map; [F9] supplies measurability of the paired kernel integrand. The Lipschitz bound in [F1] gives $\|\Phi Z-\Phi W\|\le2ML_\varepsilon T'\|Z-W\|$ on each interval. Choose $T'<1/(2ML_\varepsilon)$ (any finite $T'$ if $L_\varepsilon=0$); [F3] gives a unique fixed point. Its endpoint has finite first moment by the weighted path norm, so the same construction restarts there; finitely many intervals cover $[0,T]$.

The fixed point defines the curve in [F2]. The positive and negative label masses remain fixed, and its signed integral defines $u_t(x)=\int K_\varepsilon(x-y)d\omega_t(y)$. The integrable path supremum and [F6] give dominated continuity in $t$; [F1] gives spatial Lipschitz constant at most $ML_\varepsilon$ and at most linear growth.

By [F4], the velocity field has a unique maximal flow from each point. The linear-growth estimate and [F5] bound every trajectory on $[0,T]$ by a finite constant depending on its initial point, $T$, $M$, and $\varepsilon$. A bounded trajectory has a limit at any finite endpoint because its derivative is bounded on the resulting compact time-state set; local existence at that endpoint extends it. Hence the maximal flow $\phi_t$ exists for all $[0,T]$. Each label path from step 2.1 solves this same ODE from its initial position, so ODE uniqueness gives $Z_t(x,s)=\phi_t(x)$ for $\lambda_0$-almost every label. Solving the time-reversed equation gives an inverse; Gronwall [F5] applied to two initial states in both time orientations makes the forward and inverse maps Lipschitz on each finite interval. Thus each time map is a homeomorphism and both Jordan parts follow that common position flow.

The initial Jordan parts are mutually singular by [A1]. The common homeomorphism in step 4.1 transports a witnessing disjoint Borel partition to a disjoint Borel partition, so their pushforwards remain mutually singular. They are therefore the Jordan parts of $\omega_t$; their masses are unchanged by pushforward under the bijection. Thus $|\omega_t|(\mathbb R^2)=\omega_0^+(\mathbb R^2)+\omega_0^-(\mathbb R^2)=M$ by [F7]. Every solution in [F2] is a fixed point of the same contraction on each subinterval, so uniqueness in [F3] gives uniqueness of the represented curve.

Let $d\ge1$, with the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. An interaction kernel is a continuous map $K:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. It is globally Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the convention used on this page if
$$|K(x,y)-K(x',y')|\le L(|x-x'|+|y-y'|)$$
for all $x,y,x',y'\in\mathbb R^d$. This implies the linear-growth estimate
$$|K(x,y)|\le |K(0,0)|+L(|x|+|y|).$$
The notation $L$ always refers to this two-variable convention; the stability factor below is therefore $2L$.

Fix $T>0$, a globally Lipschitz kernel $K$ as in [[def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel]], and a Borel probability measure $\mu_0$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moment as in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]]. A characteristic solution on $[0,T]$ consists of a jointly Borel map $X:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, defined up to a $\mu_0$-null set of labels, such that $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ is absolutely continuous for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$, $X_0(x)=x$, and
$$X_t(x)=x+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(X_s(x),X_s(y))\,d\mu_0(y)\,ds$$
for $\mu_0$-almost every $x$. It transports $\mu_0$ to $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$, where $(X_t)_\#\mu_0(A):=\mu_0(X_t^{-1}(A))$. The weighted path integrability convention is $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t(x)|d\mu_0(x)<\infty$; in particular every time slice has finite first moment.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

If $\mu,
u$ are Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moments, then $\Pi(\mu,
u)$ is nonempty and $W_1(\mu,
u)<\infty$ for the definition in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]].

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Transport the prescribed coupling by the two flows: $\pi_t=(X_t,Y_t)_\#\pi_0.$ Its marginals are $\mu_t,\nu_t$. Put $D(t)=\int|X_t(x)-Y_t(y)|d\pi_0(x,y)$. This is finite and continuous by the first moments, integrable path suprema, and [F6].

Subtract the two characteristic equations and apply [F1, F5]. Integrating over the outer coupling, whose mass is one, gives $D(t)\le D_0+2L\int_0^tD(s)ds+(\eta_\mu+\eta_\nu)t.$ The inhomogeneous term is nondecreasing, so [F4] yields $D(t)\le e^{2Lt}(D_0+(\eta_\mu+\eta_\nu)t)$. Since $\pi_t$ is a coupling, this is the asserted transported-coupling bound.
The bound in step 2.1 holds for every initial coupling. Taking the infimum over their costs gives the claimed $W_1$ inequality by [F3] and the definition of $W_1$.

For a globally Lipschitz interaction kernel $K$ and $N\ge1$, the equal-probability mean-field particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K(x_i(t),x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.$$
Its empirical probability measure is $\mu_N(t)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$.

For a mollified two-dimensional Biot-Savart kernel $K_\varepsilon$ from [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]] and real weights $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_N$, the weighted signed vortex particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\sum_{j=1}^N\Gamma_jK_\varepsilon(x_i(t)-x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,$$
with vorticity measure $\omega_N(t)=\sum_i\Gamma_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$. If $\Gamma_i=1/N$ and $K(x,y)=K_\varepsilon(x-y)$, the first system is the probability special case. The weighted signed system is a first-order Biot-Savart model.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By [F2] and the ODE in the Statement, $\frac d{dt}\sum_i\Gamma_i\varphi(x_i(t)) =\sum_{i,j}\Gamma_i\Gamma_j\nabla\varphi(x_i(t))\cdot K_\varepsilon(x_i(t)-x_j(t)) +\sum_i\Gamma_i\nabla\varphi(x_i(t))\cdot g(t,x_i(t)).$ All sums are finite, so integrating this equality in time is valid.

Expanding the two signed-measure integrals on the right of the Statement gives exactly the two finite sums in step 1.1. The left side is the weighted test sum at times $t$ and $0$, so integration of step 1.1 proves the identity.

Repeated positions cause no undefined regularized kernel evaluations; the proof differentiates finite signed sums without positivity. Exact current Statement anchor: Let $x_i:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^2$ be $C^1$ trajectories with fixed real weights $\Gamma_i$, and let $g:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be a common continuous force correction. Suppose
$$\dot x_i(t)=\sum_{j=1}^N\Gamma_jK_\varepsilon(x_i(t)-x_j(t))+g(t,x_i(t)),$$
where $K_\varepsilon$ is the mollified kernel in [[def-mean-field-and-weighted-vortex-particle-systems]]. For $\omega_N(t)=\sum_i\Gamma_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$ and every $\varphi\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^2)$,
