Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. An explicit $s$-stage Runge–Kutta tableau consists of a positive integer $s$, real coefficients $a_{ij}$, $b_i$, and $c_i$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $j\ge i$, and
$$c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}\qquad(1\le i\le s).$$
The finite row sum is empty, hence $c_1=0$.

For a step size $h>0$ from an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, compute in order
$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
The strict lower-triangular condition makes each stage depend only on already computed slopes; no implicit stage equation is solved. If every stage is defined, the candidate output is
$$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$

The procedure accepts an exact right-hand-side evaluation oracle that returns either the value $f(t_i,Y_i)$ or an evaluation-failure status. Before each query it checks $(t_i,Y_i)\in D$. It returns domain-failure with the first failing stage if that check fails, evaluation-failure with the stage index if the oracle fails, and domain-failure at output if $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$. Otherwise it returns success with $(t+h,y^+)$. In the exact mathematical model the oracle returns $f$ at every point of $D$; the failure branch records only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On success this is a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

The following are the explicit Runge–Kutta tableaus in the convention of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]].

Forward Euler has $s=1$, $A=(0)$, $b=(1)$, and $c=(0)$.

Explicit midpoint has $s=2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(0,1)$, and $c=(0,1/2)$.

The classical four-stage Runge–Kutta method has $s=4$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0&0&0\\[2pt]0&1/2&0&0\\[2pt]0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)$, and $c=(0,1/2,1/2,1)$.

Each displayed $c_i$ is the row sum required in the definition of an explicit tableau. These tableaus specify the stage equations; their order and scalar stability functions are proved separately.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Put $\delta=|u-v|$ and let $d_i=|K_i(t,u)-K_i(t,v)|$. The stage times are identical for the two starting states. The stage equations [F1]-[F2] and the uniform state-Lipschitz assumption give, in order, $d_1\le L\delta,\quad d_2\le L(1+hL/2)\delta,\quad d_3\le L(1+hL/2+h^2L^2/4)\delta,$ and $d_4\le L(1+hL+h^2L^2/2+h^3L^3/4)\delta.$ Each bound follows by substituting the preceding stage bound into $|f(t_i,Y_i(u))-f(t_i,Y_i(v))|\le L|Y_i(u)-Y_i(v)|$.

The output formula in [F1]-[F2] gives $|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)|\le\left(1+hL+\frac12(hL)^2+\frac16(hL)^3+\frac1{24}(hL)^4\right)\delta\le e^{hL}\delta.$ For $h\le h_0$, $e^{hL}-1=\int_0^{hL}e^sds\le hLe^{Lh_0}$, so $e^{hL}\le1+L_*h$. This proves the claim.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. Write $\nabla U$ for its Euclidean gradient, and let $\epsilon>0$.

For $a,b\in\mathbb R$, define the **force kick** and **drift shear**
$$K_a(q,p)=(q,p-a\nabla U(q)),\qquad D_b(q,p)=(q+bM^{-1}p,p).$$
The one-step leapfrog map is
$$\Phi_\epsilon=K_{\epsilon/2}\circ D_\epsilon\circ K_{\epsilon/2},$$
where composition is read right to left. For a finite integer $L\ge1$, its $L$-step map is $\Phi_\epsilon^L$. Define the momentum flip $R(q,p)=(q,-p)$ and the flipped proposal map $T_{\epsilon,L}=R\circ\Phi_\epsilon^L$.

Each kick and drift is a continuous bijection with inverse $K_{-a}$ or $D_{-b}$, respectively. These finite maps use only $\nabla U$ and do not require a solution of Hamilton's ODE. The classical derivative of a force kick is not part of this definition: for merely $U\in C^1$, $\nabla U$ need not be differentiable.

Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $V\in C^1(Q,\mathbb R)$, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite matrix. Use the force-kick $K_a$ and drift $D_b$ already defined in [[def-leapfrog-step-map]], with $U$ there replaced by $V$. The local kick is the restriction of $K_a$ to $Q\times\mathbb R^d$. The local drift is the restriction of $D_b$ to
$$\{(q,p):q\in Q,\ q+bM^{-1}p\in Q\}.$$

For a signed step $h$, the local leapfrog map is the restriction of $K_{h/2}\circ D_h\circ K_{h/2}$ to the states for which all three intermediate configurations lie in $Q$. Its output is defined only on that admitted set. This definition changes the configuration domain of the published map; it does not redefine the global leapfrog map or assert that the local map is complete.

Under the hypotheses of [[lem-canonical-kick-and-drift-shears-have-symplectic-jacobians]], every admitted local leapfrog step and every admitted kick-then-drift symplectic Euler step has a $C^1$ Jacobian satisfying $D\Phi^TJD\Phi=J$ on its open admitted domain. The result concerns symplecticity, not energy conservation.

Let $d\ge1$, $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $V\in C^3(Q)$, and $M$ symmetric positive definite. Set $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$ and $F(q,p)=(M^{-1}p,-\nabla V(q))$. Fix $T>0$ and $h=T/N$ with $N\ge1$. Suppose the exact solution, numerical states, all kick/drift intermediate states, and every line segment used below lie in one compact convex tube $K\Subset Q\times\mathbb R^d$, with the derivatives of $F$ through order two bounded there. For $z_0$ in that tube, write $e_n^E$ for the error of iterated kick-then-drift symplectic Euler and $e_n^V$ for the error of iterated local leapfrog relative to the exact solution at $t_n=nh$. Write $\Psi_h^E$ and $\Psi_h^V$ for their admitted one-step maps and $\varphi_h$ for the exact flow. For sufficiently small $h$, constants $C_E,C_V,L$ independent of $h,N,n$ satisfy
$$\|\Psi_h^E(z)-\varphi_h(z)\|\le C_Eh^2,\qquad \|\Psi_h^V(z)-\varphi_h(z)\|\le C_Vh^3$$
for admitted $z\in K$, and whenever $nh\le T$,
$$e_n^E\le e^{LT}e_0+C_ETe^{LT}h,\qquad e_n^V\le e^{LT}e_0+C_VTe^{LT}h^2.$$
Thus symplectic Euler has global order one and leapfrog has global order two on the stated controlled tube. No unconditional domain-admissibility claim is made.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: Write the kick and drift as $K_{h/2}$ and $D_h$. Their inverses are $K_{-h/2}$ and $D_{-h}$. Since the composition is $K_{h/2}\circ D_h\circ K_{h/2}$, its inverse on the image is $K_{-h/2}\circ D_{-h}\circ K_{-h/2}$, exactly the admitted local step with signed size $-h$. This proves reversibility on the partial-map domains.

The potential $V_\varepsilon$ is smooth on the collision-free open set. The admitted local partial map therefore satisfies the hypotheses of [F2], which proves symplecticity. Under the compact convex tube and derivative assumptions in the Given clause, [F3] gives $e_n\le e^{LT}e_0+C_VTe^{LT}h^2$; exact initialization has $e_0=0$, so the finite-time global error is at most $C_VTe^{LT}h^2$.

On every admitted open kick domain the kick $K_a(q,p)=(q,p-a\nabla V_\varepsilon(q))$ has derivative $\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\-aD^2V_\varepsilon(q)&I\end{pmatrix}$. The drift $D_b(q,p)=(q+bp,p)$ has derivative $\begin{pmatrix}I&bI\\0&I\end{pmatrix}$. Both are block triangular with identity diagonal blocks, so each has determinant one by [F4]. The local composition is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism from its open admitted domain onto its open image, and multiplicativity [F4] gives determinant one for the composition. Applying [F5] to the map and its inverse yields equality of Lebesgue measures for every measurable set and its image.

Steps 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 prove reversibility, symplecticity and local volume preservation; the bound derived from [F3] proves order two on precisely the stated tube. No energy-conservation or modified-energy conclusion is used.

citations.quote: Input real endpoints $a,b,c,d$, integer panel counts $n_x,n_y$, and an exact evaluation oracle that, when queried at a point, returns either a value in $\mathbb R^2$ or evaluation-failure. First, if $a\ge b$ or $c\ge d$, return invalid-domain without querying the oracle. Next, if either panel count is odd or is less than two, return invalid-panel-count without querying the oracle. For the remaining inputs set $R=[a,b]\times[c,d]$, $h_x=(b-a)/n_x$, $h_y=(d-c)/n_y$, $x_i=a+ih_x$ for $0\le i\le n_x$, and $y_j=c+jh_y$ for $0\le j\le n_y$. Query the oracle at every grid point in lexicographic order with $i$ first and $j$ second, storing the returned values. If a query fails, stop at the first such point and return evaluation-failure with that point. Otherwise, for each $j$ form the continuous piecewise-linear interpolant through the stored values $F(x_i,y_j)$ and apply [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] componentwise in $x$ to this interpolant, obtaining $G_j=Q_xF(\cdot,y_j)$. Form the continuous piecewise-linear interpolant through the stored $G_j$ and apply the same valid Simpson procedure componentwise in $y$ to obtain $Q_yG=Q_yQ_xF$. Each interpolant is queried only at its stored grid nodes, so no new oracle call is needed. Both calls to the supplier use strictly ordered endpoints and even panel counts at least two. This is an exact-real procedure; termination and force-accuracy bounds are established in [[thm-tensor-simpson-force-error]], and floating-point roundoff is outside its scope.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be an even integer, and put $h=(b-a)/n$. If
$f\in C^4([a,b])$, set $M_4=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f^{(4)}(x)|$. Then the value
$Q_S(f;a,b,n)$ of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] satisfies

$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_S(f;a,b,n)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)h^4}{180}M_4.$$

The integral is the Riemann integral. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature
bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.

Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and an evaluation function $f$.
If $a\ge b$ or $n<2$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the
remaining inputs require $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ to be evaluable at every
point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the procedure returns
invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Invalid endpoints or panel counts return immediately without queries. Otherwise, the grid is finite, and any failed query returns immediately. If no query fails, each supplier call uses an evaluable interpolant, admissible panel counts and a finite sum, so the evaluator returns a vector. For the valid inputs in the error bound, there are exactly $(n_x+1)(n_y+1)$ grid points; the exact oracle returns $F$ at each, so none of the valid-input queries fails. The remaining supplier calls use evaluable interpolants, even positive panel counts and finite sums. Thus the evaluator terminates with a vector after the stated number of oracle queries. Fix a component $F_k$, $k=1,2$, and write $I_x,I_y$ for exact integration and $S_x,S_y$ for the composite Simpson operators. Add and subtract $I_yS_xF_k$: $I_yI_xF_k-S_yS_xF_k=I_y(I_x-S_x)F_k+(I_y-S_y)S_xF_k.$ The maxima in the Statement are finite by [F4]. For each fixed $y$, [F2] bounds the first one-dimensional error by $(b-a)h_x^4M_{40}/180$; integrating in $y$ gives $(b-a)(d-c)h_x^4M_{40}/180$.

The $y$ derivative commutes with the finite $x$-weighted sum. Applying [F2] to each fixed $x$ and then summing the nonnegative Simpson weights from [F3] bounds the second term by $(b-a)(d-c)h_y^4M_{04}/180$. Thus each coordinate error is at most $E=|R|(h_x^4M_{40}+h_y^4M_{04})/180$.
If both coordinate errors have absolute value at most $E$, their Euclidean norm is at most $(E^2+E^2)^{1/2}=\sqrt2E$. Substitution of the value of $E$ from step 2.1 proves the Statement.

Under the smoothness and compact-tube hypotheses of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]], the forward Euler, explicit midpoint, and classical four-stage tableaus of [[def-euler-midpoint-rk4-tableaus]] have uniform local orders at least one, two, and four, respectively.

For the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$, set $z=h\lambda$. The corresponding stability functions, defined by $y^+=R(z)y$, are
$$R_{\mathrm E}(z)=1+z,\qquad R_{\mathrm M}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2},\qquad R_{\mathrm{RK4}}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}+\frac{z^3}{6}+\frac{z^4}{24}.$$
The absolute stability region of a listed method is $\{z\in\mathbb C:|R(z)|\le1\}$. On the negative real axis, the Euler and midpoint regions are exactly $[-2,0]$. No maximal real interval is asserted here for RK4.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $f:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^m$ be uniformly $L$-Lipschitz in its state variable on a set containing every stage generated by the classical RK4 step of [[def-euler-midpoint-rk4-tableaus]] from any two admitted starting states $u,v$ at the same base time $t$. Assume all these stage evaluations are defined, and let $\Psi_h(t,\cdot)$ be the resulting one-step map for $0<h\le h_0$. Then
$$|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)|\le(1+L_*h)|u-v|,\qquad L_*=Le^{Lh_0}.$$

Let $T>0$, $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$, $h=T/N>0$, $p\in\mathbb R$ with $p\ge1$, and $C_0,C,L\ge0$. Real powers of the positive base $h$ are as in [[def-real-power]]. If nonnegative real numbers $e_0,\ldots,e_N$ satisfy
$$e_0\le C_0h^p,\qquad e_{n+1}\le(1+Lh)e_n+Ch^{p+1}\quad(0\le n<N),$$
then, when $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, when $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}e_n\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the autonomous augmentation $(t,X)'=(1,f(t,X))$. The time component is integrated exactly by RK4 because its weights sum to one; the state component therefore has the same exact-start defect order. The tube and derivative assumptions in the Given clause make the defect uniform, so [F2] gives the bound $C_4h^5$.

Put $E_k=|X_k-x(t_k)|$ for the numerical and exact grid states. Applying [F3] to the admitted exact/numerical start pair, using [F6] for the state Lipschitz premise, bounds the one-step map difference by $(1+L_*h)E_k$. The exact-start local defect is at most $C_4h^5$ by step 1.1 and [F2]. The Euclidean triangle inequality [F5] therefore gives $E_{k+1}\le(1+L_*h)E_k+C_4h^5$, with $E_0=0$.
Apply [F4] with $p=4$, $C_0=0$, $C=C_4$, $L=L_*$, and the recurrence from step 2.1. Its $L_*>0$ and $L_*=0$ cases are exactly the displayed bound.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Write $\|F\|_{L^1}:=\int_{\mathbb R^2}|F(x)|dx$ and let $\|g\|_{L^\infty}$ be the essential supremum of $|g|$. There is a constant $C_\rho<\infty$, independent of $\varepsilon>0$, such that
$$\|K_\varepsilon-K\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_\rho\varepsilon.$$
Consequently, for every bounded measurable vorticity density $\omega$,
$$\|(K_\varepsilon-K)*\omega\|_{L^\infty}\le C_\rho\varepsilon\|\omega\|_{L^\infty}.$$
This is an error estimate at fixed $\varepsilon$; it does not prove a singular-limit theorem for the particle dynamics.

derivations.claim: If $M=0$, then $\omega_0=0$ and [F6] gives $\sum_i|\Gamma_i|=0$, hence every particle weight is zero. Thus both vorticity measures vanish at time $T$. By [F5], $E_0=0$ and the displayed bound is zero; hence the conclusion holds. Suppose $M>0$. By [F1] and the bound $\|\omega_t\|_\infty\le W$, the exact Euler flow, when written with interaction kernel $K_\varepsilon$, has an additive force defect at most $C_\rho\varepsilon W$. The tensor evaluator contributes the second additive defect at most $\eta_q$ by [F2].

By consolidation and disjointness of the positive and negative atomic supports, the finite measures $\sum_{\Gamma_i>0}\Gamma_i\delta_{x_i^0}$ and $\sum_{\Gamma_i<0}|\Gamma_i|\delta_{x_i^0}$ are mutually singular positive measures whose difference is $\omega_N^0$. Uniqueness of Jordan parts and [F6] therefore give $\sum_i|\Gamma_i|=M$. Couple each exact force-evaluated particle trajectory to its RK4 trajectory using the same signed particle label. The state error in [F4] is the Euclidean norm on the full particle state, so each particle-block displacement is no larger than $C_{RK}h^4$. Apply [F3] to the exact Euler characteristic flow and the common sign-preserving force-evaluated regularized flow, using initial split cost $E_0$, total variation mass $M$, and summed defect $C_\rho\varepsilon W+\eta_q$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,

derivations.claim: Let $S=\{Y_1,\ldots,Y_N\}$ be the empirical support. It contains at most $N$ vertices, so $\mu_M(V_M\setminus S)\ge1-N/2^M$. Distinct vertices of $V_M$ have Euclidean distance at least one.

In any coupling of $\mu_M$ to $\nu_N$, every point of $V_M\setminus S$ must send its mass to a point of $S$, at cost at least one per unit mass. Hence every coupling costs at least $1-N/2^M$, and taking the infimum in [F1] proves the bound. If $2^M\ge2N$, it is at least $1/2$; choosing $N$ arbitrarily large and then such an $M$ rules out a uniform dimension-free $C N^{-1/2}$ bound.

$$W_1(\mu,

u)}\int_{\mathbb R^d	imes\mathbb R^d}|x-y|\,d\pi(x,y).$$
This definition makes no assertion that the infimum is attained. It applies only to probability measures with finite first moment; it is not a distance assigned here to a general signed measure.

Let $\omega,
u$ be finite signed Borel measures on $\mathbb R^d$ such that $|\omega-
u|(\mathbb R^d)<\infty$. For each bounded Lipschitz test function, integration against $\omega-
u$ is defined by [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]; boundedness and finite total variation make every test in the following set integrable. Set $\|\phi\|_\infty:=\sup_x|\phi(x)|$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(\phi):=\sup_{x
e y}|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|/|x-y|$, using the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Define the bounded-Lipschitz dual discrepancy
$$d_{BL}(\omega,
u):=\sup\left\{\left|\int\phi\,d(\omega-
u)ight|:\|\phi\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}(\phi)\le1ight\}.$$
The integral bound by total variation shows this supremum is finite. This page uses only the displayed dual quantity and makes no separate metric-separation claim. No Jordan decomposition, positivity, or probability normalization is needed.

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $d\ge1$, with the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. An interaction kernel is a continuous map $K:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. It is globally Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the convention used on this page if
$$|K(x,y)-K(x',y')|\le L(|x-x'|+|y-y'|)$$
for all $x,y,x',y'\in\mathbb R^d$. This implies the linear-growth estimate
$$|K(x,y)|\le |K(0,0)|+L(|x|+|y|).$$
The notation $L$ always refers to this two-variable convention; the stability factor below is therefore $2L$.

For a globally Lipschitz interaction kernel $K$ and $N\ge1$, the equal-probability mean-field particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K(x_i(t),x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.$$
Its empirical probability measure is $\mu_N(t)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$.

For a mollified two-dimensional Biot-Savart kernel $K_\varepsilon$ from [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]] and real weights $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_N$, the weighted signed vortex particle system is
$$\dot x_i(t)=\sum_{j=1}^N\Gamma_jK_\varepsilon(x_i(t)-x_j(t)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,$$
with vorticity measure $\omega_N(t)=\sum_i\Gamma_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$. If $\Gamma_i=1/N$ and $K(x,y)=K_\varepsilon(x-y)$, the first system is the probability special case. The weighted signed system is a first-order Biot-Savart model.

Let $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ solve the equal-probability system of [[def-mean-field-and-weighted-vortex-particle-systems]] on $[0,T]$, and put $\mu_N(t)=N^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(t)}$. Then for every $\varphi\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^d)$,
$$\int\varphi d\mu_N(t)-\int\varphi d\mu_N(0) =\int_0^t\int\nabla\varphi(x)\cdot\left(\int K(x,y)d\mu_N(s)(y)\right)d\mu_N(s)(x)ds.$$
Thus the empirical measure satisfies the same weak transport equation exactly, with no particle quadrature error in this identity.

Let $K$ have two-variable Lipschitz constant $L$ as in [[def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel]], and let $\mu_t,

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $d\ge1$. For Borel probability measures $\mu,
u$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moments $\int |x|\,d\mu(x)<\infty$ and $\int |y|\,d
u(y)<\infty$, let $\Pi(\mu,
u)$ be the set of Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d	imes\mathbb R^d$ whose first and second marginals are $\mu$ and $
u$. Define
$$W_1(\mu,
u):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,
u)}\int_{\mathbb R^d	imes\mathbb R^d}|x-y|\,d\pi(x,y).$$
This definition makes no assertion that the infimum is attained. It applies only to probability measures with finite first moment; it is not a distance assigned here to a general signed measure.

Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and probability measure has the meaning of [[def-probability-measure]].

If $\mu,
u$ are Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite first moments, then $\Pi(\mu,
u)$ is nonempty and $W_1(\mu,
u)<\infty$ for the definition in [[def-p-one-wasserstein-one]].

Assume Countable Choice and the radial compactly supported mollifier of [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]]. Write $\|F\|_{L^1}:=\int_{\mathbb R^2}|F(x)|dx$ and let $\|g\|_{L^\infty}$ be the essential supremum of $|g|$. There is a constant $C_\rho<\infty$, independent of $\varepsilon>0$, such that
$$\|K_\varepsilon-K\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_\rho\varepsilon.$$
Consequently, for every bounded measurable vorticity density $\omega$,
$$\|(K_\varepsilon-K)*\omega\|_{L^\infty}\le C_\rho\varepsilon\|\omega\|_{L^\infty}.$$
This is an error estimate at fixed $\varepsilon$; it does not prove a singular-limit theorem for the particle dynamics.

Let $a<b$, $c<d$, let $n_x,n_y\ge2$ be even integers, and set $R=[a,b]\times[c,d]$, $h_x=(b-a)/n_x$, $h_y=(d-c)/n_y$. If $F\in C^4(R,\mathbb R^2)$ and
$$M_{40}=\max_R|\partial_x^4F|,\qquad M_{04}=\max_R|\partial_y^4F|,$$
then the tensor evaluator of [[alg-tensor-simpson-force-evaluator]] satisfies
$$\left|\int_R F-Q_yQ_xF\right|\le\frac{\sqrt2\,|R|}{180}\bigl(h_x^4M_{40}+h_y^4M_{04}\bigr),\qquad |R|=(b-a)(d-c).$$
On every declared input, if each oracle query returns a value or evaluation-failure, the evaluator terminates with its specified status. For the valid inputs above, with the exact oracle returning $F$ at every grid point, the evaluator terminates and returns a vector after exactly $(n_x+1)(n_y+1)$ oracle queries. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature bound, not a roundoff estimate.

Let $K$ have two-variable global Lipschitz constant $L$ as in [[def-globally-lipschitz-mean-field-kernel]]. Let $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$ and $
u_t=(Y_t)_\#
u_0$ be probability curves from finite-first-moment initial laws, with absolutely continuous characteristic paths satisfying
$$\dot X_t(x)=\int K(X_t(x),X_t(z))d\mu_0(z)+r_\mu(t,x),\qquad \dot Y_t(y)=\int K(Y_t(y),Y_t(w))d
u_0(w)+r_
u(t,y)$$
for almost every time and almost every label, with $X_0(x)=x$ and $Y_0(y)=y$. Assume additionally the weighted path integrability conditions $\int\sup_{s\le T}|X_s|d\mu_0<\infty$ and $\int\sup_{s\le T}|Y_s|d
u_0<\infty$. Assume the measurable label defects satisfy $|r_\mu|\le\eta_\mu$ and $|r_
u|\le\eta_
u$ on $[0,T]$. For every prescribed initial coupling $\pi_0$ of cost $D_0$, its transport by the two characteristic paths has cost at time $t$ at most
$$e^{2Lt} igl(D_0+(\eta_\mu+\eta_
u)t igr).$$
Consequently $W_1(\mu_t,
u_t)\le e^{2Lt} igl(W_1(\mu_0,
u_0)+(\eta_\mu+\eta_
u)t igr)$. The estimate is first proved for each coupling; no optimal plan is assumed.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$, finitely many vortex weights, $T>0$, and the regularized finite-particle vector field of [[def-mean-field-and-weighted-vortex-particle-systems]], possibly with an added common smooth force correction $g_q(t,X,x_i)$ for spatial force quadrature. Suppose the resulting nonautonomous state field $f(t,X)$ is jointly $C^4$ on an open time-state domain, with derivatives through order four bounded on a common compact convex tube $\mathcal T$ compactly contained in that domain. Assume the exact path, RK4 grid states, and every RK4 stage lie in that tube for $h=T/N\le h_0$, and the common force correction is included in these bounds. Let $C_4$ be a uniform exact-start defect constant, so the local defect is at most $C_4h^5$ as in [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]]. Let $L_*$ be the stability constant from [[lem-classical-rk4-map-is-lipschitz-on-a-controlled-tube]], so the one-step factor is $1+L_*h$. For exact initialization, the state errors $E_k$ satisfy
$$\max_{0\le k\le N}E_k\le \begin{cases} C_4\dfrac{e^{L_*T}-1}{L_*}h^4,&L_*>0,\\ C_4Th^4,&L_*=0. \end{cases}$$
The tube and stage-admissibility assumptions are conditional; no invariance or global numerical-domain claim is made. The constant $C_4$ may depend on $\varepsilon$, particle count, the quadrature field, and the tube.

For every step $k$, assume all RK4 stages generated from both the exact start $x(t_k)$ and the numerical start $X_k$ lie in $\mathcal T$, and both one-step maps are defined. Let $L$ be a uniform operator-norm bound for $D_Xf$ on $\mathcal T$ and set $L_*=Le^{Lh_0}$, as in the stability lemma. The only admitted start pair used in the stability estimate at step $k$ is $(x(t_k),X_k)$.

Assume Countable Choice and the mollifier of [[def-mollified-biot-savart-vortex-kernel]]. For every $\varepsilon>0$, $G_\varepsilon$ and $K_\varepsilon$ are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and there is $C_\rho<\infty$ independent of $\varepsilon$ such that
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}\|DK_\varepsilon(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}.$$
Consequently $K_\varepsilon$ is globally Lipschitz with constant at most $C_\rho\varepsilon^{-2}$.

derivations.claim: Write the exact Euler characteristic velocity as the mollified interaction plus residual $(K-K_\varepsilon)*\omega_t$, whose norm is at most $C_\rho\varepsilon W$ by [F2]. The quadrature particle field is the mollified interaction plus a common residual of norm at most $\eta_q$ by [F3]. Fix any initial coupling with cost $D_0\le E_0+\delta$, where $\delta>0$. Transport it by the Euler flow and the exact quadrature-force particle flow. By [F4], the resulting coupling has cost at time $T$ at most $e^{2L_\varepsilon T}\bigl(E_0+\delta+T(C_\rho\varepsilon W+\eta_q)\bigr).$

Use the same initial particle label in the exact quadrature-force path and the RK4 path. The RK4 state error in [F5] is Euclidean on the full particle state, so each particle-block displacement is at most $C_{RK}h^4$. Since the initial nodes are distinct, partition the coupling by its second coordinate and label each part by its unique particle index. Push this labelled coupling through the exact Euler flow in the first coordinate and the RK4 particle map in the second. The resulting coupling from the Euler law to the RK4 empirical law has cost at most the step 1.1 bound plus $C_{RK}h^4$. Thus it bounds their $W_1$. Since $\delta>0$ was arbitrary, let $\delta\downarrow0$ to obtain $W_1(\omega_T,\omega_{N,h}^{\varepsilon,q}(T)) \le e^{2L_\varepsilon T}\bigl(E_0+T(C_\rho\varepsilon W+\eta_q)\bigr)+C_{RK}h^4.$ This same-sign estimate uses probability transport and has no AC hypothesis; it makes no uniform claim as $\varepsilon\to0$.
